entities.name: Bernardus Papiensis
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Bernardus Papiensis, an influential Italian canonist and bishop, played a pivotal role in the systematic organization of medieval canon law, particularly through his landmark work, the *Compilatio prima*. Born in Pavia in the mid-12th century (exact date unknown), he rose through ecclesiastical ranks to serve as Bishop of Faenza from 1195 to 1198, and subsequently as Bishop of Pavia from 1198 until his death on September 25, 1213. His efforts to codify the burgeoning volume of papal legislation emanating from the nascent papal monarchy significantly streamlined legal practice and study across Latin Christendom.

His most enduring contribution, the *Compilatio prima* (c. 1191–1192), was a comprehensive collection of papal decretals issued after Gratian's *Decretum* (c. 1140) and canons from various councils. This work, also known as the *Breviarium extravagantium*, was the first of the *Quinque compilationes antiquae* (Five Old Compilations) and quickly gained official recognition, being adopted as a textbook at Bolognese law schools. Bernardus meticulously arranged the material into five books covering judges, judgments, clergy, marriage, and crime, a structure that would profoundly influence subsequent canon law compilations.

The *Compilatio prima* became indispensable for legal scholars and ecclesiastical courts, providing a standardized and accessible body of law that helped solidify the authority of the papacy and rationalized judicial processes throughout the Catholic Church. Its rigorous methodology and clear organization set a new benchmark for legal codification, paving the way for definitive collections like the *Decretales* of Gregory IX in 1234. Bernardus's work thus served as a crucial transitional phase, bridging Gratian's initial synthesis and the comprehensive codifications that defined the zenith of medieval canon law.
